grammar.title: Present perfect for experience: ever, never, been and gone
grammar.summary: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about experiences in your life up to now, when we don't say exactly when they happened. Use 'ever' in questions and 'never' in negative sentences.
grammar.summaryMn: Амьдралынхаа туршид (одоог хүртэл) олж авсан туршлагынхаа тухай, яг хэзээ болсныг хэлэхгүйгээр ярихад present perfect (have/has + V3) хэрэглэнэ. Асуултад 'ever' (хэзээ нэгэн цагт), үгүйсгэлд 'never' (хэзээ ч) хэрэглэнэ.
structure: Positive: I/you/we/they have ('ve) + past participle · he/she/it has ('s) + past participle → I've visited Japan. · She's flown a lot.
Negative: haven't/hasn't + past participle, or have/has + never + past participle → I haven't seen the sea. · I've never ridden a camel.
Question: Have/Has + subject + (ever) + past participle? → Have you ever been to Korea? — Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
been to = went and came back · gone to = went and is still there
Past participles: regular -ed (visited, travelled) · irregular (be → been, go → gone, fly → flown, see → seen, eat → eaten, ride → ridden)

grammar.title: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar.summary: Use the present perfect for experiences and past actions when we don't say when, or when the time period is not finished (today, this year). Use the past simple when we say or know exactly when something happened (yesterday, last summer, in 2020, two days ago).
grammar.summaryMn: Хэзээ болсныг хэлээгүй эсвэл хугацаа нь дуусаагүй (today, this year) үед present perfect хэрэглэнэ. Яг хэзээ болсныг хэлсэн эсвэл мэдэгдэж байгаа (yesterday, last summer, in 2020, two days ago) үед past simple хэрэглэнэ.
structure: Present perfect: have/has + past participle — no finished time → I've been to Seoul.
Past simple: verb + -ed or irregular past — finished time → I went to Seoul last year.
Finished time (past simple): yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child
Unfinished time (present perfect): today, this week, this year, in my life
Questions about details (When? Where? How long?) use the past simple → When did you go?

usage.use: Start with the experience (present perfect), then give details (past simple)
usage.example: I've been to Japan. I went there in 2022 and stayed for two weeks.
usage.useMn: Эхлээд туршлагаа (present perfect), дараа нь дэлгэрэнгүйг (past simple) хэлнэ

usage.useMn: Дууссан цаг дурдсан эсвэл тодорхой бол → past simple

usage.useMn: Хугацаа нь дуусаагүй бол → present perfect

usage.use: Questions with 'When…?' use the past simple

pronunciation.title: Weak forms: have, has, been and to
pronunciation.explanation: In natural speech, small grammar words are usually weak — short, quiet and with the vowel /ə/ or /ɪ/. In present perfect sentences, 'have' often sounds like /həv/ (or just /v/), 'has' like /həz/ (or /z/), 'been' like /bɪn/ and 'to' like /tə/. The important words — ever, never, the main verb, the place — are stressed. In short answers at the end of a sentence we use the strong form: 'Yes, I HAVE' /hæv/.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Байгалийн ярианд жижиг туслах үгс ихэвчлэн сул хэлбэрээр — богино, намуухан, /ə/ эсвэл /ɪ/ эгшигтэй дуудагдана. Present perfect-д 'have' нь /həv/ (эсвэл зөвхөн /v/), 'has' нь /həz/ (эсвэл /z/), 'been' нь /bɪn/, 'to' нь /tə/ болно. Чухал үгс (ever, never, үндсэн үйл үг, газрын нэр) өргөлттэй. Харин өгүүлбэрийн төгсгөл дэх богино хариултад хүчтэй хэлбэр хэрэглэнэ: 'Yes, I HAVE' /hæv/.

items.display: have → /həv/: Have you ever…? = /həv jə ˈevə/
items.tip: Don't say a strong /hæv/ at the start of a question. Keep it short and quick.

items.display: Strong form in short answers: Yes, I HAVE. /hæv/
items.tip: At the end of a sentence, 'have' is strong and clear.

items.display: haven't / hasn't are always strong: No, I HAVEN'T.

lessons.title: Twelve hours on a bus
objectives: Use 11 words and collocations for journeys and public transport
Understand the main idea, details and order of events in a travel blog

warmup.intro: Think about the longest journey you have ever made. How did you travel, and how long did it take?

questions.prompt: What do you call a person who travels on a bus or plane but isn't the driver or pilot?
The blog in this lesson is called 'Twelve Hours on the Bus to Mörön'. What do you think it is about?
options: How to become a bus driver
Problems with city buses in Ulaanbaatar
A traveller's long bus trip to northern Mongolia
questions.explanation: Mörön is a town in northern Mongolia, near Lake Khövsgöl.

vocabulary.definition: the act of travelling from one place to another, especially over a long distance
vocabulary.mn: аялал, зорчилт (нэг газраас нөгөөд очих зам)
examples: The journey from Ulaanbaatar to Mörön takes about twelve hours by bus.
Have a safe journey and call me when you arrive!
vocabulary.mistake: Don't say 'a travel'. 'Travel' is a verb or an uncountable noun. Say 'a journey' or 'a trip'.
vocabulary.note: A 'trip' is the whole visit (going, staying and coming back). A 'journey' is the travelling part.

vocabulary.definition: the place where someone or something is going
examples: We reached our destination late at night.
Lake Khövsgöl is a popular destination for summer holidays.
vocabulary.note: Stress the fourth syllable: des-ti-NA-tion.

vocabulary.definition: a person who is travelling in a vehicle but is not driving it or working on it
examples: The bus was full, with more than forty passengers on board.
Passengers must keep their seatbelts on until the plane stops.
vocabulary.mistake: The 'g' sounds like /dʒ/ and there is an /n/ before it: PAS-in-jer, not 'pas-sen-ger' with a hard g.

vocabulary.definition: buses, trains and other vehicles that everyone can pay to travel on
examples: I usually use public transport to get around the city.
Public transport in Ulaanbaatar is cheap but often crowded.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Transport' is uncountable here: say 'public transport', not 'public transports'.
vocabulary.note: American English: public transportation.

vocabulary.definition: the money you pay to travel by bus, train, plane or taxi
examples: How much is the train fare to Darkhan?
Taxi fares usually go up at night.
vocabulary.mistake: Use 'fare' for transport, 'fee' for services (a course fee) and 'price' for things in shops.
vocabulary.note: 'Fare' and 'fair' sound exactly the same: /feə/.

vocabulary.definition: full of people
examples: The buses are always crowded during rush hour.
We avoided the crowded beaches and found a quiet one.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't say 'It was many people.' Say 'It was crowded' or 'There were a lot of people.'

vocabulary.definition: a situation in which something happens later than planned; to make something late
examples: There was a two-hour delay because of the snow.
Our flight was delayed by fog.
vocabulary.mistake: Use the passive for transport: 'The flight was delayed', not 'The flight delayed'.

vocabulary.definition: to start a journey
examples: We set off at six to avoid the traffic.
What time do you need to set off tomorrow?
vocabulary.note: Irregular: set – set – set. Common in both speech and writing.

vocabulary.definition: in or to a foreign country
examples: Have you ever travelled abroad?
My cousin is studying abroad, in Korea.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Abroad' is an adverb, so there is no preposition: say 'go abroad', not 'go to abroad'.

vocabulary.definition: visiting famous or interesting places as a tourist
examples: We spent the afternoon sightseeing in the old town.
Did you have time for any sightseeing?
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'go sightseeing', not 'go to sightseeing' — the same as 'go shopping' and 'go swimming'.

vocabulary.definition: the natural features of a place, such as mountains, rivers and forests, especially when they are beautiful
examples: The scenery on the road to Khövsgöl is amazing.
We stopped the car to enjoy the scenery.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Scenery' is uncountable: 'the scenery is beautiful', not 'the sceneries are beautiful'.

reading.title: Twelve Hours on the Bus to Mörön
text: Most foreign tourists who visit Lake Khövsgöl in northern Mongolia hire a private jeep with a driver. It's comfortable, but it isn't cheap. I'm a student from New Zealand on a tight budget, so I decided to use public transport instead. My friends in Ulaanbaatar told me I was crazy. Now that I've done it, I can say it was the best journey of my whole trip.

The bus was supposed to leave the Dragon bus station at eight in the morning, but we waited forty minutes for two passengers who were late, so we finally set off at twenty to nine. The fare to Mörön was about 50,000 tögrög — less than twenty US dollars for almost 700 kilometres. The bus was crowded: every seat was taken, and there were bags of flour, boxes of vegetables and even a small fridge in the aisle.

That wasn't the only delay. Somewhere after Bulgan, one of the tyres went flat, and the driver changed it at the side of the road. Nobody complained. Instead, an old woman offered everyone aaruul — hard, dried curd — and the teenager next to me practised his English by asking me questions about rugby.

The scenery was the best part. For hours we drove past green hills, rivers and huge herds of horses, and we stopped at small roadside cafés for milk tea and khuushuur. We reached our destination just after nine in the evening, more than twelve hours after we left. I was exhausted, but very happy.

The next day I took a minivan to the lake and spent three days hiking and sightseeing. Would I take the bus again? Absolutely. If you travel abroad and really want to understand a country, don't just look at it through the window of a private car. Get on the bus with everyone else — just bring snacks, a warm jacket and a lot of patience.

vocabulary.definition: to travel around a place to learn about it
examples: We spent the whole day exploring the old part of the city.
I'd love to explore the Gobi Desert one day.
vocabulary.mistake: No preposition after 'explore': 'explore the city', not 'explore in the city'.

vocabulary.definition: from or in the area you are talking about; a person who lives in that area
examples: Have you tried the local food?
We asked a local for directions to the monastery.
vocabulary.note: As a noun, 'a local' / 'the locals' is informal and common in travel talk: 'Ask the locals.'

vocabulary.definition: something you buy to help you remember a place you visited
examples: I bought a small felt camel as a souvenir.
The souvenir shops near the square are very expensive.
vocabulary.mistake: The stress is at the end: soo-vuh-NEER, not SOO-ve-nir.

vocabulary.definition: travelling cheaply with your things in a bag on your back, usually staying in cheap places
examples: She went backpacking around South-East Asia after university.
Backpacking is a cheap way to see the world.
vocabulary.note: A person who does this is a 'backpacker'.

vocabulary.definition: special or unusual and easy to remember
examples: Our trip to the Gobi was the most memorable holiday I've ever had.
The eagle festival was a memorable day for everyone.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't confuse 'memorable' (easy to remember) with 'memory' (the noun): 'a memorable trip', not 'a memory trip'.

vocabulary.definition: very special because it will probably happen only once
examples: Seeing the eagle festival was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime chance, so don't miss it.
vocabulary.note: Use hyphens when it comes before a noun: 'a once-in-a-lifetime trip'.

vocabulary.definition: the tired feeling you have after a long flight to a place where the time is very different
examples: I've never had such bad jet lag as after my flight to New York.
It took me three days to get over the jet lag.
vocabulary.mistake: It is uncountable: 'I had terrible jet lag', not 'I had a terrible jet lag'.
vocabulary.note: Adjective: 'I'm still jet-lagged.'

vocabulary.definition: sad because you are far from home and miss your family and friends
examples: I felt homesick during my first month in Seoul.

vocabulary.mistake: 'Homesick' is not an illness. 'I'm homesick' means 'I miss home', not 'I'm sick at home'.

vocabulary.definition: a feeling of confusion when you visit or live in a very different culture
examples: Many students experience culture shock when they first move abroad.
The biggest culture shock for me was how quiet people were on the trains.
vocabulary.note: 'Reverse culture shock' is the strange feeling when you come back home after a long time abroad.

speaking.prompt: A new English-speaking colleague asks you: 'Do you travel much? Where have you been?' Talk about your travel experiences — places you've been to, things you've never done, and your most memorable trip.

I've been there twice, and both times I've slept in a ger and ridden a camel. Seeing the stars at night was a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Have I ever felt homesick? vocabulary.definition: the bags and suitcases you take with you when you travel
examples: How much luggage are you taking?
My luggage didn't arrive in London.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Luggage' is uncountable: say 'two pieces of luggage' or 'two bags', not 'two luggages'.

vocabulary.definition: the area at an airport where people check your bags and your body before you fly
examples: It took us forty minutes to get through security.
You can't take bottles of water through security.

vocabulary.definition: the place at an airport or border where officers check what you are bringing into a country
examples: We went through customs and collected our bags.
Customs officers opened my suitcase and looked inside.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Customs' (with -s) = гааль. 'A custom' (without -s) = a tradition, заншил.

vocabulary.definition: the act of leaving a place, especially at the start of a journey
examples: Please arrive at the airport two hours before departure.
Check the departures board to find your gate.
vocabulary.note: At airports the signs say 'Departures' (leaving) and 'Arrivals' (coming in).

vocabulary.definition: to say that something that was planned will not happen
examples: If the weather is bad, the airline may cancel the flight.
I had to cancel my hotel booking.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't mix up 'cancel' (it will not happen) and 'delay' (it will happen later).
vocabulary.note: British spelling: cancelled, cancelling. American: canceled, canceling.

vocabulary.definition: a short stay in a place between two parts of a journey, especially a long flight
examples: We had a three-hour stopover in Seoul.
Tickets are often cheaper if there's a stopover.
vocabulary.note: American English usually says 'layover'.

vocabulary.definition: the passage between rows of seats on a plane, bus or train
examples: Would you like a window seat or an aisle seat?
Please keep your bags out of the aisle.
vocabulary.mistake: The 's' is silent: say /aɪl/, exactly like 'I'll'.

vocabulary.definition: a public statement that gives people information, for example at an airport
examples: Listen carefully to the announcements for your gate number.
The captain made an announcement about the weather in Beijing.
vocabulary.mistake: We 'make' an announcement, not 'do' or 'say' an announcement.

listening.title: Is this a window seat?
listening.context: Nomin is flying abroad for the first time. Her friend Dave, who travels a lot for work, meets her at the airport in Ulaanbaatar.

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: Nomin! Over here! So, are you nervous? It's your first time flying, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Yes, I've never been on a plane before. I've checked in online, but I'm not sure what to do next.

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: OK, first we need to drop off your luggage. Have you got your boarding pass on your phone?

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Yes, it's here. Seat twenty-three C. Is that a window seat?

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: No, C is an aisle seat. That's actually good on a long flight. You can get up without climbing over people.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Right. My flight goes to London, but there's a stopover in Istanbul. Do I need to collect my suitcase there?

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: No, your bag goes all the way to London. You only go through customs when you arrive in the UK.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: That's a relief. What about security? I've heard it takes ages.

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: It's usually quite quick here. Just take your laptop out of your bag, and don't take any water through.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Oh no, I've got a big bottle of water in my backpack!

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: Well, drink it now or leave it here! Your departure time is ten fifteen, so you've got plenty of time.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: And what happens if the first flight is delayed or cancelled, and I miss my connection?

lines.speaker: Dave
lines.text: Don't worry, the airline will put you on the next flight. Just listen to the announcements and check the screens for your gate. They usually start boarding about forty minutes before departure.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: OK. Thanks, Dave. I feel much better now.

vocabulary.definition: a place to live or stay, such as a hotel room or a flat
examples: The price includes flights and accommodation.

vocabulary.mistake: In British English it's uncountable: 'accommodation', not 'accommodations'. Spelling: two c's and two m's.
vocabulary.note: American English often uses the plural 'accommodations'.

vocabulary.definition: an arrangement to keep a room, table or seat for you
examples: I have a reservation for two nights under the name Bold.

vocabulary.mistake: Mongolian 'захиалга' can mean 'order' or 'booking'. For hotels and restaurants say 'reservation' or 'booking', not 'order'.

vocabulary.definition: a cheap place to stay, often with shared rooms, popular with young travellers
examples: We stayed in a hostel near the station for ten dollars a night.

vocabulary.mistake: Don't confuse 'hostel' /ˈhɒstl/ with 'hotel' /həʊˈtel/: the stress is on different syllables.

vocabulary.definition: the desk in a hotel or office where people arrive and ask for information
examples: Please leave your key at reception when you go out.

vocabulary.mistake: Say 'at reception' (usually without 'the'), not 'in the reception'.
vocabulary.note: American English often says 'the front desk'.

vocabulary.definition: to pay your bill and leave a hotel

vocabulary.definition: to say that something is good and that someone should try it
examples: I'd recommend this guesthouse to anyone visiting Kharkhorin.

vocabulary.mistake: Say 'recommend a hotel to me' or 'Can you recommend a hotel?', not 'recommend me a hotel'. Spelling: one c, two m's.

vocabulary.definition: good or useful enough to spend time or money on
examples: The hotel was expensive, but it was worth the money.
The old monastery is definitely worth visiting.
vocabulary.mistake: Use -ing after 'worth': 'worth visiting', not 'worth to visit'.

vocabulary.definition: warm, comfortable and pleasant, often in a small space
examples: The ger was small but warm and cosy.
We found a cosy little café next to the hotel.
vocabulary.note: American spelling: cozy.

vocabulary.definition: completely clean
examples: Our room was spotless and the bed was very comfortable.
The bathrooms were spotless.
vocabulary.note: Very common in hotel reviews. Don't say 'very spotless' — use 'absolutely spotless'.

vocabulary.definition: costing more than it is really worth
vocabulary.mn: үнэ нь хэт өндөр, дэмий үнэтэй
examples: The food at the airport is always overpriced.
The rooms were nice but a bit overpriced.
vocabulary.note: More negative than 'expensive': it means the price is not fair.

phrases.phrase: I have a reservation under the name…
phrases.meaning: used when you arrive at a hotel or restaurant to say who the booking is for
phrases.whenToUse: At a hotel reception or restaurant when you arrive. Polite and natural in any situation.
phrases.example: Hi, I have a reservation under the name Bat-Erdene, for three nights.

phrases.meaning: Is breakfast part of the price?
phrases.whenToUse: When you book or check in. You can use it for anything: 'Is Wi-Fi included?', 'Is parking included?'
phrases.example: Is breakfast included, or do we pay extra?

phrases.meaning: a very polite way to ask for something
phrases.whenToUse: For requests that are a little special, such as a late check-out or a quieter room. More polite than 'Can I…?' and good in formal emails too.
phrases.example: Would it be possible to check out a bit later, at about one o'clock?

phrases.meaning: it was expensive, but so good that the money was well spent
phrases.whenToUse: In reviews and conversations about something you paid for. Avoid it in formal complaints.
phrases.example: The hotel wasn't cheap, but it was worth every penny.

phrases.meaning: used to introduce a negative point after positive ones
phrases.whenToUse: In reviews and opinions, to give a balanced view. In speech people often say 'The only problem was…'.
phrases.example: On the downside, the walls were thin and the street was noisy at night.

phrases.meaning: used to give a final opinion after thinking about everything
phrases.whenToUse: At the end of a review, story or conversation. In formal writing 'Overall, …' is also good.
phrases.example: All in all, it was a great place to stay.

writing.promptMn: Өөрийн байрлаж байсан зочид буудал, хостел, эсвэл жуулчны баазын тухай онлайн богино сэтгэгдэл бичээрэй: хаана байдаг, хэзээ байрласан, өрөө болон ажилчдын тухай, нэг давуу, нэг сул талыг бичээд бусдад санал болгох эсэхээ хэлээрэй.

writing.sample:
Great ger camp near Kharkhorin ★★★★☆

I've stayed in a lot of ger camps, but this one is special. My husband and I stayed here for two nights last August. Our ger was cosy and spotless, and the beds were really comfortable. The staff at reception were friendly and helped us book a horse-riding trip. Breakfast was included, and the local yoghurt was delicious.

On the downside, the showers were quite far from the gers, and dinner was a bit overpriced. All in all, it was worth every penny — the views of the Orkhon Valley at sunset were amazing. I'd recommend this accommodation to anyone who wants peace and quiet.

reading.title: The Return of the Night Train
text: Twenty years ago, many people thought night trains in Europe were finished. Cheap airlines were growing fast, and a flight from Paris to Rome often cost less than a train ticket. One by one, railway companies stopped their sleeper services. Today, however, night trains are coming back.

The main reason is simple: more and more passengers want to travel without flying. A night train from Vienna to Hamburg produces much less CO2 than a plane. But the environment is not the only reason. 'On a plane you lose a whole day,' says Lena Hoffmann, a teacher from Berlin who has taken the night train to Vienna four times. 'On a night train, you have dinner, go to sleep and wake up at your destination. It feels like you've travelled for free.'

Of course, night trains are not perfect. A bed in a private compartment can be more expensive than a flight, and delays are common because the trains often travel through several countries. Some passengers also complain that they can't sleep because of the noise and the movement.

Still, railway companies are optimistic. Austria's national railway has bought dozens of new sleeper carriages, and new routes have opened between cities like Brussels, Berlin and Prague. For many travellers, the slow journey has become part of the holiday.

listening.title: Checking in at a guesthouse
listening.context: Sarah, a tourist from England, arrives late in the evening at a small guesthouse in Kharkhorin.

lines.text: Good evening, welcome to Orkhon Guesthouse. How can I help you?

lines.text: Hi. I have a reservation under the name Sarah Miller, for two nights.

lines.text: Sure, here you are. Sorry I'm so late. My bus from Ulaanbaatar was delayed by three hours.

lines.speaker: Temuujin
lines.text: Oh, that's no problem. Have you been to Kharkhorin before?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: No, I haven't. It's my first time in Mongolia, actually. I arrived in Ulaanbaatar on Monday.

lines.speaker: Temuujin

lines.speaker: Sarah

lines.speaker: Temuujin

Hi Jake,

Great news that you're coming to Mongolia! I've been to a lot of places here, but my favourite destination is Lake Khövsgöl in the north. I went there last July with my cousins. We rode horses, went kayaking and slept in a ger camp next to the water. The scenery was amazing.

The journey by bus is very long, so I'd recommend flying to Mörön and then taking a minivan to the lake. It's more expensive, but it's worth it. For accommodation, book a ger camp early because they're often full in summer.

Let me know if you need any help!

speaking.sample: If you want to travel from Ulaanbaatar to Beijing, you can fly or take the train. The plane is much faster — the flight only takes about two hours, and sometimes the fare isn't much higher. On the other hand, the train takes about thirty hours, but in some ways it's more comfortable: you can walk around, sleep in a proper bed and enjoy the scenery of the Gobi. I've taken the train to Beijing once, when I was a student, and it was a really memorable journey. I've flown there three times for work. Personally, I prefer the plane when I'm busy, but for a holiday I'd choose the train, because the journey is part of the experience.
